### Go version

go version go1.28-devel_651ec67c3b Fri Sep 25 09:02:19 2026 -0700 (master), building for `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64`. go1.27.1 generates the same code, so this isn't a regression.

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOOS=linux
GOARCH=arm64
GOARM64=v8.0
CGO_ENABLED=0
GOEXPERIMENT=
```

Cross-compiled from linux/amd64 and benchmarked on linux/arm64 (Neoverse N1).

### What did you do?

A loop multiplying by a 64-bit constant that doesn't fit an arm64 immediate, compared with the same loop loading the constant from a variable:

```go
package repro

const prime = 0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463

//go:noinline
func Hash(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {
	for i, v := range src {
		dst[i] = uint32((v * prime) >> 45)
	}
}

var primeVar uint64 = prime

//go:noinline
func HashVar(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {
	p := primeVar
	for i, v := range src {
		dst[i] = uint32((v * p) >> 45)
	}
}
```

### What did you see happen?

`Hash` rebuilds the constant with `MOVD` + 3×`MOVK` on every iteration, even though the loop uses only a handful of registers. (From `go tool objdump`, with branch targets relabelled for readability.)

```
loop:
	LSR	$45, R5, R5
	MOVW	R5, (R0)(R2<<2)
	ADD	$1, R2, R2
	CMP	R2, R4
	BLE	done
	MOVD	(R3)(R2<<3), R5
	MOVD	$25699, R6
	MOVK	$(47013<<16), R6
	MOVK	$(48348<<32), R6
	MOVK	$(53019<<48), R6
	MUL	R6, R5, R5
	CMP	R2, R1
	BHI	loop
```

`HashVar` loads it once before the loop and keeps it in `R2`:

```
	ADRP	..., R27
	MOVD	1232(R27), R2
loop:
	LSR	$45, R6, R6
	MOVW	R6, (R0)(R5<<2)
	ADD	$1, R5, R5
	CMP	R5, R4
	BLE	done
	MOVD	(R3)(R5<<3), R6
	MUL	R2, R6, R6
	CMP	R5, R1
	BHI	loop
```

On a Neoverse N1 (4096 elements, one pinned core, `-count 10`), `HashVar` is 20% faster:

```
     │   Hash    │              HashVar               │
     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base               │
Hash   5.161µ ± 0%   4.128µ ± 0%  -20.02% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

For comparison, amd64 makes the same choice, rebuilding the constant inside the loop, but there it is a single `MOVQ $imm64` with no dependency chain:

```
loop:
	SHRQ	$0x2d, DX
	MOVL	DX, 0(AX)(CX*4)
	INCQ	CX
	CMPQ	SI, CX
	JLE	done
	MOVQ	0(DI)(CX*8), DX
	MOVQ	$0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463, R8
	IMULQ	R8, DX
	CMPQ	BX, CX
	JA	loop
```

so the same comparison on a Ryzen 5 5600X is much smaller:

```
     │   Hash    │              HashVar              │
     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base              │
Hash   2.037µ ± 7%   1.956µ ± 2%  -3.98% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

### What did you expect to see?

The constant built once outside the loop and kept in a register, as with `HashVar`.

As far as I can tell, this is because `MOVDconst` is marked `rematerializeable: true` ([ARM64Ops.go#L413](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/_gen/ARM64Ops.go#L413)), and [`(*Value).Rematerializeable`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/regalloc.go#L165) only looks at the opcode. So the register allocator treats a constant that takes 4 instructions to build the same as one that takes 1. That's the right call on amd64, where `MOVQ $imm64` is always one instruction, but not on arm64. The `MOVDconst` ops for riscv64, ppc64, mips64 and loong64 carry the same flag. I haven't checked their code generation.

Motivation: this showed up in the zstd encoder's match-finder hashing in klauspost/compress. https://github.com/klauspost/compress/pull/1230 works around it by loading the hash primes from a package-level `var` on arm64 only (`hashPrimesInRegs = runtime.GOARCH == "arm64"`). That accounts for most of the PR's +6–8% encode throughput on Graviton2/3/4. On amd64 the same workaround is slower, because rebuilding the constant costs a single `MOVQ` and holding it adds spills in a loop that already has high register pressure. So the workaround has to be per-architecture, and it would be better fixed in the compiler.

Loop-invariant code motion (#63670) wouldn't help on its own: SSA constants already live in the entry block, outside the loop, and the register allocator re-emits them at each use.

items.body:
### Go version

go version go1.27.1 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
n/a
```

### What did you do?

We noticed a substantial slowdown in microbenchmarks for a specialized hash table implementation.

Here's a minimized reproducer:

```
package slowload

import (
	"encoding/binary"
	"testing"
)

//go:noinline
func f(k [4]byte) uint32 {
	q := k
	return binary.BigEndian.Uint32(q[:])
}

func BenchmarkIndex(b *testing.B) {
	k := [4]byte{1, 2, 3, 4}
	for b.Loop() {
		f(k)
	}
}
```

### What did you see happen?

There's a slowdown on amd64:

```
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: github.com/cespare/misc/slowload
cpu: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X 12-Core Processor
         │ amd64/126.txt │            amd64/127.txt            │
         │    sec/op     │   sec/op     vs base                │
Index-24     1.906n ± 3%   2.185n ± 3%  +14.66% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

If we look at the generated code, we see:

1.26.7:

```
  MOVL  0x4(SP), CX
  BSWAP CX
```

1.27.1:

```
  MOVZX 0x22(SP), BX
  ROLW  $0x8, BX
  MOVZX BX, BX
  MOVZX 0x21(SP), SI
  MOVQ  CX, 0x4(SP)
  MOVL  DX, 0xc(SP)
  SHLL  $0x10, SI
  ORL   SI, BX
  MOVZX 0x4(SP), CX
  SHLL  $0x18, CX
  ORL   BX, CX
```


On arm64 (my test machine is Graviton 5) we see a much more dramatic slowdown:

```
goos: linux
goarch: arm64
pkg: github.com/cespare/misc/slowload
         │ arm64/126.txt │            arm64/127.txt             │
         │    sec/op     │   sec/op     vs base                 │
Index-48     1.856n ± 0%   4.229n ± 1%  +127.86% (p=0.000 n=10)
```

The generated code:

1.26.7:

```
  MOVWU 40(RSP), R1
  MOVW  R1, 20(RSP)
  MOVWU 20(RSP), R1
  REVW  R1, R0
```

1.27.1:

```
  MOVWU  40(RSP), R1
  MOVHU  42(RSP), R2
  REV16W R2, R2
  UBFX   $0, R2, $16, R2
  MOVBU  41(RSP), R3
  MOVW   R1, 20(RSP)
  ORR    R3<<16, R2, R1
  MOVBU  20(RSP), R2
  ORR    R2<<24, R1, R0
```

### What did you expect to see?

No regression.

The weird-looking array copy (`q := k`) is important. In our real code, the copy happens due to a function call.

I bisected this regression to [CL 748200](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/748200) ("cmd/compile: forward small Load through Move to avoid redundant copies"). Issue #80980 is also complaining about a regression from that CL (I'm not sure if this should be considered a dup of #80980 or not).

/cc @Dorbmon @randall77

items.title: cmd/compile: simd.Float32s.Neg rebuilds its sign-bit constant on every loop iteration

labels.name: NeedsFix
labels.description: The path to resolution is known, but the work has not been done.

labels.name: compiler/runtime
labels.description: Issues related to the Go compiler and/or runtime.

items.body:
### Go version

go version go1.27.1 linux/amd64 / gotip

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOOS=linux
GOARCH=amd64
GOAMD64=v1
GOEXPERIMENT=simd
```

### What did you do?

Found this while working on https://github.com/mauri870/loopvec.

Compiled and disassembled a loop that calls `Float32s.Neg`:

```go
package main

import "simd"

func neg(dst, a []float32) {
	for i := 0; i < len(dst); {
		v, n := simd.LoadFloat32sPart(a[i:])
		v.Neg().StorePart(dst[i:])
		i += n
	}
}

func main() {
	a := make([]float32, 100)
	d := make([]float32, 100)
	neg(d, a)
}
```

```
GOEXPERIMENT=simd go build -o neg .
go tool objdump -s 'main\.neg@simd512$' neg
```

`neg` is a dispatcher that picks `neg@simd128`, `neg@simd256` or `neg@simd512`
on every call; the loop body lives in the width-specific clone.


### What did you see happen?

`Neg` lowers to an XOR with a sign-bit vector, but the instructions that
build that vector are emitted at the use site, inside the loop body, instead
of once before the loop. On `go1.27.1` the relevant part of `neg@simd512`
is:

```
4a3898  ...                          ; loop head (the back edge jumps here)
4a38d6  VMOVDQU64 0(DX), Z1          ; full-width load
4a3922  MOVL $-0x80000000, DX        ; constant rebuilt every iteration
4a3927  VMOVD DX, X2
4a392b  VPBROADCASTD X2, Z2
4a3937  VPXORD Z2, Z1, Z1            ; the actual negation
4a3947  VMOVDQU64 Z1, 0(R9)          ; full-width store
4a394d  JMP 0x4a3898                 ; back edge, before the constant rebuild
```

On gotip (`go1.28-devel_2ca679b1f1`) the same sequence appears, at shifted
addresses:

```
49cfd2  ...                          ; loop head
49d016  VMOVDQU64 0(DX), Z0
49d05c  MOVL $-0x80000000, DX        ; constant rebuilt every iteration
49d061  VMOVD DX, X1
49d065  VPBROADCASTD X1, Z1
49d071  VPXORD Z1, Z0, Z0
49d07e  VMOVDQU64 Z0, 0(R9)
49d084  JMP 0x49cfd2                 ; back edge, before the constant rebuild
```

In both, the `MOVL $-0x80000000` / `VMOVD` / `VPBROADCASTD` sequence sits
between the loop head and the back-edge jump target, so it re-executes every
iteration. The result is correct; it is three extra instructions and a
dependency chain per iteration for a value that never changes.

### What did you expect to see?

The sign-bit constant materialized once before the loop and kept live in a
register across iterations, the way a user-hoisted constant already is.
